answers.1: The main objects are: decimal literals (0.1, 0.2, 0.3); the double, a 64-bit binary format that holds a whole number of at most 53 binary digits times a power of two; the stored value, which is the double nearest a literal; the gap, which is the distance between neighboring doubles (u = 2^-54 between 0.25 and 0.5); the error, which is the stored value minus the decimal; the + operation, giving an exact sum and then a rounded sum; the tie and the round-half-to-even rule; `==`; printing as the shortest decimal that rounds back to the double; and the Decimal type.
answers.2: Each literal is rounded to its stored value, a double on a grid. The grid's gap depends on the size of the number. `+` adds the stored values exactly, then rounds the result onto the grid. The rule for ties decides which neighbor it lands on. `==` compares the two doubles bit for bit. Printing shows the shortest decimal that rounds back to that double, which hides small errors unless two doubles need to be told apart.
answers.3: 0.1 and 0.2 cannot end in binary because 10 has a factor of 5, so both are stored slightly too high, while 0.3 is stored slightly too low. Their exact sum falls halfway between two doubles, the tie rounds up to the double just above stored 0.3, and so `==` returns false.
answers.4: The key variable is whether the decimal's denominator contains a factor of 5, meaning it is not a power-of-two fraction. If every value is a power-of-two fraction (0.5, 0.25, 0.75), the stored error is zero, the exact sum is already a double, and `==` is true. A second variable is the number of digits kept. With more digits the gap gets smaller, but a repeating binary fraction still has to be cut. The text implies this but does not discuss changing the digit count.
answers.5: Assumption or simplification: the text ignores the sign and exponent bits and treats a double as 'a whole number of at most 53 binary digits times a power of two'. Established fact: 0.1 + 0.2 prints 0.30000000000000004, and in units of u the stored 0.3 is 5404319552844595 while the sum rounds to …596.
answers.6: A double can only hold a binary fraction with at most 53 significant bits. 1/10 has a factor 5 in its denominator, so its binary expansion never ends and it has to be rounded, much as 1/3 is in decimal. Stored 0.1 and 0.2 are each slightly above their true values, and stored 0.3 is slightly below. Adding the stored 0.1 and 0.2 exactly gives a value halfway between two doubles, and the round-to-even rule picks the one just above stored 0.3, so the two differ by one gap and `==` is false. Printing shows the shortest decimal that identifies a double, which is why 0.1 prints as 0.1 but the sum needs 17 digits.
answers.7: The hardest part was the table and the units of u. Fractional values in u, such as 1801439850948198.5, are confusing until you link them to 'steps allowed here = u/4'. The text also never says why the gap is exactly 2^-54 in [0.25, 0.5), which is 2^-2 × 2^-52 from the 53 digits. In the tie step, it never says outright that …596 is the even one. One worked line on the gap, and the sentence '…596 is even, …595 is odd', would have made it easier.
answers.8: It is true. 1/2, 1/4 and 3/4 have power-of-two denominators, so each is stored with zero error, and the exact sum is itself a double, so rounding changes nothing.
answers.9: No. The `+` returns the nearest double to the exact sum of its inputs, which is correct. The difference comes from the inputs, which were already rounded versions of 0.1 and 0.2, and from the fact that 0.3 was rounded independently (downward). The final rounding of the sum, a tie broken to even, is the only rounding the operation does, and it follows the rule.
answers.10: Yes, it would be true. Decimal stores base-10 digits, and 1/10 ends in base 10, so no rounding happens.
answers.11: 0.75 = 3 × 2^-2 is a whole number times a power of two, so its denominator is a power of two. 1/10 has a factor 5 in its denominator, no power of two is divisible by 5, so its binary expansion repeats forever and has to be cut.
answers.12: Both stored values err upward (+5.55e-18 and +1.11e-17), so their exact sum is 5404319552844595.5 u. That is a tie between …595 and …596, and ties go to even, so it rounds to …596. Stored 0.3 was rounded down, to …595. The two results are neighboring doubles one gap (5.55e-17) apart.
answers.13: Languages print the shortest decimal that rounds back to the same double. The text '0.1' already rounds back to stored 0.1, so one digit is enough and the error stays hidden.
